summary: The first live bench of myseliasan's sign-in surface, against a real two-instance CLUSTER (two myseliasan containers on one shared Postgres and one shared Redis, the SHIPPED posture with the rate limiter on), found that the fleet control plane had NO failed-login lockout at all and no audit trail for authentication. POST /api/auth/local-login called AuthenticateLocal and returned: the only brute-force control on the console that owns every camera in the estate was the generic rate limiter - 30 requests a minute, per source, per path, PER INSTANCE, refilling forever, never escalating, blind to one account being attacked from many addresses. The bench served 13 consecutive guesses at roughly 61ms each and then signed in with the correct password as though nothing had happened. POST /api/auth/change-password was the same shape one layer in, an unmetered password oracle for anyone holding a stolen session cookie - 11 current-password guesses went through it in a row. Both now go through the shared sharedapis.LoginGuard, wired from the same loginSecurity config block every other app reads (the block is ABSENT from this app's config.json and an absent block resolves to ON with the suite defaults, so the configuration had been promising a lockout the code never implemented), keyed on ip:<remote addr> AND user:<lowercased username>, with the per-failure delay applied, and attached to the shared cache under namespace myseliasan whenever cache.provider is redis/redis-cluster so the lockout spans the cluster rather than giving an attacker a fresh allowance per instance. A rejected NEW password on change-password is a policy refusal and is deliberately not counted, so a user holding a valid session cannot lock themselves out picking a password the policy keeps refusing. Second finding: the audit trail had never recorded a single authentication event. It records node adoptions, policy edits, key rotations and failover takeovers, so a complete brute-force run left nothing at all in the product's own record of who did what. It now writes login.success, login.failure, login.lockout (once, on the attempt that engages it) and password.change, using the same action names myidsan uses so the two trails correlate, and never the password attempted. On these entries clientIp is the PEER address rather than the X-Forwarded-For the app's other entries use - on a login entry the address is the evidence, and a forged header would also make the trail disagree with the lockout about who was attacking; a proxy's claim is kept in metadata as claimedForwardedFor, labelled as claimed rather than observed. Third finding, and the reason a checklist did not catch any of this: LoginGuard.SharesState() was added in the previous change with a comment saying the clustering preflight reads it to tell an operator the truth about their cluster, and nothing ever read it. The preflight now has a loginLockout blocker row (CheckLoginLockout, domain/shared/services/deployment.go) reporting both that a guard is switched on and that its counters are shared, with a translated label and fix hint in all four languages. Finally, the key derivation, the lockout 429 body and the loginSecurity mapping moved into domain/shared/apis (LoginGuardKeys, LoginGuardSourceKey, LoginGuardAccountKey, WriteLockoutJSON, NewLoginGuardFor) and myidsan's private copies now delegate to them, so there is one implementation of this security decision rather than two that can drift. The bench scores 36/36 against the fix and 17/36 against unfixed main, measured on one identical set of checks (KOPIV2_SKIP_BUILD=1 against a binary built from a worktree at main). A separate screen check (tools/fleetbench/uicheck_sel_lockout.js) drives the real sign-in form in headless Chrome with real keystrokes and confirms a locked-out operator is shown a translated countdown rather than the generic 'invalid username or password' - 4/4 in English, 6/6 in Malay and 6/6 in Arabic including RTL - because the server sends one English sentence and the SPA ships in four languages, so that half is invisible to any API assertion.
compatibility: Backward-compatible; no migration needed. The audit_log table is unchanged - the new entries are ordinary rows with new action names. Single-instance myseliasan installs and installs on a non-shared cache provider get the in-memory lockout only, which is exactly what an appliance needs; the shared store is attached only when cache.provider is redis/redis-cluster. OPERATIONALLY VISIBLE CHANGE: myseliasan installs that previously had no lockout now enforce one on upgrade with no configuration change, using the suite defaults the absent loginSecurity block already resolves to (8 failed attempts in 300s, then a 60s lockout doubling to at most an hour, plus a 400ms delay on every failed attempt). An operator who genuinely wants no lockout must now say so deliberately with loginSecurity.enabled=false. Failed sign-ins are also 400ms slower by design; successful ones are unchanged. A deployment behind a reverse proxy that does NOT terminate at this process will see every user share one source key, because the guard reads RemoteAddr and never the spoofable X-Forwarded-For - the account key still separates them, and terminating TLS at the app is the documented posture for the whole suite. The clustering preflight gains a row that FAILS on an install with no shared cache; that is a report of the state that install was already in, not a new restriction, and it blocks nothing but the checklist's Ready verdict. myidsan is behaviourally unchanged: its guard-key and lockout-response helpers now delegate to the shared implementations they were copied from, and it gains the same preflight row.
